summary.title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
summary.executive_summary: This study presents an optimized high-throughput freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation activity. Addressing limitations in thermal uniformity and sample throughput found in previous cuvette-based systems, the authors implemented an automated droplet generation protocol using a Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handler and a controlled-rate Asymptote VIA freezer. The system utilizes 96-deep well plates or 48 cryovials containing monodisperse aqueous droplets suspended in silicone oil. Key innovations include the use of a metal cooling plate to minimize thermal gradients and a constant cooling rate of -0.25 °C/min to ensure stochastic nucleation events are captured accurately. Results demonstrate that the new system significantly reduces well-to-well variability in freezing temperatures compared to generic freezers, achieving a p-value of 0.83 for uniformity versus 4.4×10⁻⁷ for the previous setup. The platform successfully identified ice-nucleating active (INA) droplets at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, distinguishing them from inactive controls. While the system achieved a theoretical throughput of ~3800 droplets, practical limitations regarding droplet stability during transport due to static electricity were noted. Overall, the work establishes a robust, semi-automated framework for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating particles.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents an optimized high-throughput freeze-float selection platform for measuring ice nucleation activity. Addressing limitations in thermal uniformity and sample throughput found in previous cuvette-based systems, the authors implemented an automated droplet generation protocol using a Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handler and a controlled-rate Asymptote VIA freezer. The system utilizes 96-deep well plates or 48 cryovials containing monodisperse aqueous droplets suspended in silicone oil. Key innovations include the use of a metal cooling plate to minimize thermal gradients and a constant cooling rate of -0.25 °C/min to ensure stochastic nucleation events are captured accurately. Results demonstrate that the new system significantly reduces well-to-well variability in freezing temperatures compared to generic freezers, achieving a p-value of 0.83 for uniformity versus 4.4×10⁻⁷ for the previous setup. The platform successfully identified ice-nucleating active (INA) droplets at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C, distinguishing them from inactive controls. While the system achieved a theoretical throughput of ~3800 droplets, practical limitations regarding droplet stability during transport due to static electricity were noted. Overall, the work establishes a robust, semi-automated framework for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating particles.

Research Context
Prior systems used cuvettes with low thermal conductivity. Silicone oil caused significant thermal lag in larger containers. Parallel cuvette setups resulted in non-uniform temperature results. High-throughput screening relies on miniaturization and automation. Droplet assays offer chemical compartmentalization advantages. Polydispersity in droplet size directly influences freezing temperature. A 1 mm vs 0.1 mm droplet difference causes a 2.3 °C shift. Reliable freezing temperature requires a sufficient sample number.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to expand the system to higher throughput and accuracy. Hypothesis: Automated generation will increase efficiency with fewer manipulation steps. Hypothesis: Larger sample sizes will increase measurement accuracy. Hypothesis: Controlled-rate cooling will improve temperature uniformity. Hypothesis: Robotic dispensing produces sufficiently uniform droplet volumes. Hypothesis: Constant cooling rates minimize well-to-well thermal gradients. Hypothesis: The system can distinguish INA droplets from inactive controls.

Methodological Details
The study utilized a 96 deep well plate compatible with Biomek 3000. Droplets were generated using a silicone oil buoyant layer. HFE-7500 was used as a cushion layer at the bottom. 30 × 1 L droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer. Dispensing rate was 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The system generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells. Total throughput reached up to ~3800 droplets at once. Droplet dispersion was assessed using fluorescein dye. Polydispersity was defined as standard deviation divided by mean radius. Measured polydispersity was 9.2% for the robotic system. Static electricity was removed using an Auto-set Ion Pump. Validation used 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein. Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to compare distributions. Generic freezer cooling showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷. Linear cooling reduced p-value to 0.31. Asymptote VIA freezer accommodated up to 48 cryovials. Each cryovial contained 50 L HFE-7500 cushion. Cryovials contained 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant. Control droplets were INA free milli Q water. Control droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue.

Procedures And Architectures
Automated generation replaced manual generation by repeat pipetting. Matlab program Droplet_Dispersion.m analyzed droplet diameters. Python script KStest.ipynyn compared freezing temperature distributions. Asymptote VIA freezer provided constant rate cooling. Cooling precision reached down to -0.5 °C/min. Custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording. Generic digital camera was used for image recording. Metal cooling plate achieved homogeneous cooling. Cooling rate was set to -0.25 °C/min. Freezing time range increased with linear cooling. Mean freezing time differed between cells (47.4 and 50.6 min). Asymptote freezer showed less well-to-well variability. Standard deviation in Asymptote freezer was 0.73. Overall dispersion was 36% lower in Asymptote system. Droplets with INA froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C. Inactive droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. Controlled cooling improved detection compared to commodity freezer. Mean temperature in commodity freezer was -7.5 ± 0.97 °C. Droplet stability was insufficient during transport. Static electricity caused coalescing during transfer.

Key Results
Robotic system generated 40 uniform droplets in ~15 minutes. Polydispersity of 9.2% indicated sufficiently uniform volume. Expected nucleation temperature dispersion was no more than ±0.09 °C. Generic freezer showed significant thermal gradient (p = 4.4×10⁻⁷). Linear cooling decreased thermal gradient (p = 0.31). Mean freezing time difference was 3.2 minutes (47.4 vs 50.6). Asymptote freezer showed p = 0.83 for well-to-well variability. Asymptote standard deviation was 0.73 vs 1.6 for generic. Asymptote system achieved 36% lower dispersion overall. INA droplets froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C in Asymptote. Inactive droplets froze at -12.3 °C in Asymptote. Controlled cooling improved differentiation accuracy. Commodity freezer mean temperature was -7.5 ± 0.97 °C. Theoretical throughput is ~3800 uniform 1 L droplets. Static electricity caused coalescing during system transfer.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Uniform droplet size minimizes freezing temperature variance. Constant cooling rates are critical for stochastic nucleation models. Larger sample sizes reduce confidence interval width. Metal cooling plates improve thermal homogeneity. Controlled-rate freezers reduce well-to-well variability. The system successfully distinguishes INA from non-INA. Improved accuracy allows for better detection thresholds. High throughput enables statistical robustness in measurements. Static electricity remains a barrier for portable deployment. The platform bridges microfluidics and HTS plate formats.

Contradictions And Limitations
Droplet stability was not sufficient for long-distance transfer. Static electricity from friction caused droplet coalescing. Combining generation and screening systems failed due to stability. 96-well plates suffer from cell-to-cell thermal gradients. Generic freezers show high p-values for uniformity (4.4×10⁻⁷). Linear cooling increases the range of freezing times. Mean freezing times vary between cells even with linear cooling. Transport limitations restrict the system's portability.

Claims
The Asymptote VIA freezer significantly improves thermal uniformity compared to generic freezers. Asymptote showed p = 0.83 for well-to-well variability. Asymptote dispersion was 36% lower than generic. Standard deviation dropped from 1.6 to 0.73. Generic freezer showed p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ for gradients. Controlled cooling enables accurate heterogeneous nucleation measurement.
Automated droplet generation achieves high monodispersity suitable for nucleation studies. Polydispersity was measured at 9.2%. Expected temperature dispersion was ±0.09 °C. Static electricity caused coalescing during transport. Robotic systems enable high-throughput screening of thousands of droplets.

Data And Code Availability
Source Code S1 for Droplet_Dispersion.m is available. Source Code S3 for KStest.ipynyn is available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Linear cooling reduced thermal gradients compared to constant temperature. Multi-head dispensers can accelerate the generation rate. HFE-7500 cushion layer prevents wall contact destabilization.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows 96 deep well plate compatibility. Figure 1 C-E shows droplet dispersion analysis. Figure 2 shows freezing behavior in generic freezer. Figure 3 shows thermal gradient in 96-well plate. Figure 4 shows freezing temperatures in Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows well-to-well variability in Asymptote. Figure 6 shows overall dispersion comparison.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a high-throughput freeze-float system with automated dispensing and controlled cooling. 2. The strongest evidence is the reduction in thermal variability (p=0.83) and improved detection accuracy. 3. The future path involves resolving static electricity issues for portable deployment.
